newsitem.title: UK: Violence paves way to new IRA truce.
newsitem.headline: Violence paves way to new IRA truce.

text.p: The Irish Republican Army on Saturday announced a new ceasefire in its 28-year-old war to end British rule over Northern Ireland.
The last IRA ceasefire was called on August 31 1994 and lasted for 17 months.
This is a chronology of the drive for peace over the past three years:
Sept 1, 1994 - IRA starts ceasefire.
Oct 14 - Pro-British "Loyalist" guerrillas start truce.
Dec 9 - British officials hold first public meeting with Sinn Fein, political wing of IRA, in 22 years.
Feb 22, 1995 - British Prime Minister John Major and Irish Premier John Bruton unveil joint framework document on a Northern Irish political settlement.
March 22 - British minister holds first talks with Protestant political parties linked to loyalist guerrillas.
May 10 - Britain ends 23-year ban on ministerial talks with Sinn Fein.
June 18 - Sinn Fein breaks off exploratory peace talks with Britain, angered at British attitude to IRA arms.
Sept 5 - Ireland abruptly postpones summit talks with Britain, refusing to link future all-party peace talks to London's insistence that IRA guerrillas disarm.
Sept 19 - Spokesmen for loyalist gunmen hold their first peace talks with the Irish government.
Nov 28 - London and Dublin announce "twin-track" process setting end of February 1996 for start of all-party talks and announcing commission to study arms issue.
Nov 30 - U.S President Bill Clinton visits Northern Ireland.
Dec 15 - International commission under former U.S. senator George Mitchell tries to resolve weapons row.
Dec 19 - Sinn Fein holds first ministerial talks.
Jan 24 - Mitchell proposes talks alongside phased surrender of guerrilla weapons. Instead, Major proposes elections in Northern Ireland to pave way for talks.
Feb 9 - IRA abandons ceasefire. A bomb blast in east London's docklands area injures 100 people and kills two.
Feb 18 - IRA bomb explodes on bus in London killing the guerrilla who was carrying it and injuring eight others.
Feb 28 - Major and Bruton revive peace process and announce June 10 date for all-party talks. They say Sinn Fein will stay outside unless the IRA ceasefire restarts.
May 30 - Elections in Northern Ireland for Peace Talks Forum see Sinn Fein increase share of vote to 15 percent.
June 10 - Multi-party talks on the future of Northern Ireland begin in Belfast, but Sinn Fein is excluded.
June 15 - IRA bomb explodes in the centre of Manchester, northern England causing enormous damage and injuring more than 200.
June 28 - Three mortar bombs fired at British army barracks in Osnabrueck, Germany.
July 6 - Police ban Protestant Orange Order march planned for the next day through a Catholic area of Portadown. Northern Ireland is gripped by a wave of rioting.
July 11 - Police reverse ban on march and allow 2,000 Protestants to walk along the Garvaghy Road in Portadown.
July 12 - After a night of Catholic riots in which three policemen were shot and wounded, tens of thousands of Protestants parade their British loyalty.
Oct 7 - IRA stages first bombing in Northern Ireland for more than two years, attacking British army headquarters. A soldier is killed and 30 other people injured.
February 12 - British soldier Stephen Restorick shot dead by an IRA sniper at a Northern Ireland checkpoint.
March 26 - IRA detonate two bombs on railway in northern England, bringing chaos to the network.
March 30 - Pro-British Loyalists plant car bomb outside Sinn Fein office in Belfast.
April 3 - British police find two bombs on motorway in northern England.
April 5 - IRA force the postponement of Grand National horse race at Aintree with bomb threats.
April 10 - Police reservist Alice Collins shot in the back by IRA sniper in Londonderry.
April 18-29 - Series of explosions and bomb warnings cause travel chaos in England.

May 1 - Labour wins landslide British election victory. Sinn Fein President Gerry Adams and his lieutenant Martin McGuiness win seats but refuse to swear oath of allegiance to Queen Elizabeth and are barred from parliament.
May 21 - Britain's new Labour government ends 16-month ban on contacts with Sinn Fein and holds talks.
June 6 - Centre-right opposition led by Bertie Ahern's Fianna Fail wins narrow victory in Irish election.

June 21 - British Prime Minister Tony Blair warns Sinn Fein time is running out for it to join talks after a restoration of the IRA ceasefire. A bomb explodes in Belfast under a car carrying a prominent member of an Irish republican group, injuring three.
June 16 - IRA guerrillas shoot dead two Northern Irish policemen. Britain breaks off contact with Sinn Fein.
June 25 - Blair unveils new proposals including an independent commission to oversee the scrapping of guerrilla arms in parallel with talks on a political settlement.
June 26 - Ahern becomes Irish prime minister after winning the backing of independents including Sinn Fein.
June 30 - Blair meets Ahern to discuss Northern Ireland.
July 6 - Protestant Orange Order march goes ahead at Portadown after talks to avert it fail. The march sparks new rioting in nationalist areas across the province.
July 7 - Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam condemns "orchestrated" nationalist violence.
July 9 - Britain sends 500 more troops to Belfast.
July 10 - Orange Order calls off four contentious marches through nationalist areas.
July 11 - Seven people - two teenagers and five members of the security forces -- injured in Belfast attacks.
July 12 - Orangemen stage peaceful marches to mark anniversary of Battle of the Boyne in 1690. Police fire plastic bullets at rioters in Londonderry and Belfast.
July 13 - Northern Ireland police find huge haul of home-made explosives, favoured weapon of the IRA.
July 14 - Britain acknowledges official contacts with Sinn Fein to clarify conditions for the group's eventual admission to peace talks.
July 15 - An 18-year-old Catholic girl, Bernadette Martin, is shot dead in a sectarian killing.
Northern Ireland peace talks resume in Belfast with Unionists angered by British contacts with Sinn Fein.
July 18 - Sinn Fein asks IRA to restore truce, saying Britain has removed some obstacles to negotiations.
July 19 - IRA announces "unequivocal" ceasefire to start at noon (1100 gmt) Sunday July 20.
